citations.translation: I am going to dress you in my purple garb

notes.text: Greek πορφύριον. Note how the stressed second vowel of the Greek is rendered by /ū/ in Syriac but by /ī/ in JPA. This difference is generally the norm in such words, indicating perhaps that the Syriac was borrowed from an earlier (or a different) dialect of koine where the front vowel was still rounded, the JPA from an unrounded form. Alternatively it may simply be argued that the change /ū/ > /ī/ occurred under the influence of Greek differently in Syriac and JPA, as indicated by such Semitic words as prwg, prwgɁ n.m. : chick.

citations.translation: [=MT וְעַל גַּנָּתוֹ יֹנַקְתּוֹ תֵצֵא]

notes.text: The targumist is being splendidly playful here, even more so than usual. By choosing this form, all of the following literary and lexical allusions are covered with one fell swoop: the source BH term ‏‏גַּנָּתוֹ and both its content and its similarity to גנון, "bridal chamber;" and the form פורינא, "bridal litter" and its BH cognate ‏אַפִּרְיוֹן and its context in Song of Songs 3:9. All of this play is echoed in (or echoes) PsJon Dt.32:50: אתקין ליה פוריינא וקטר ליה גננא בגויה. See also s.v. pwryn #2.

notes.text: DJPA treats the plural of this word simply as a form of pry in JPA (with much justification, also so for CPA!), but to judge by the existence of two clearly different forms of the singular in Syriac, as well as the appearance of clearly singular forms of this word in PTA, CPA, Mandaic and JBA, this has become a separate word in at least some if not most post-OfA dialects. In Babylonian it is probably the only form. The situation is thus as follows: Prior to the later dialects, only pry, but unfortunately, there are no clear attestation of a plural before that time. In colloquial Palestinian dialects generally sg. pĕrī, sg. emph. pēryā, pl. pērīn with some contamination from Syriac and Babylonian in the texts; Syriac: both forms, but the meanings have been divided: this form is for the fruit of trees as well as figurative meanings while the form ܦܪܝܐ is used only in the figurative senses; Babylonian only pērā. LJLA is like Palestinian (i.e. sg. abs./constr=פרי) but only has pērā for the sg. emph. KWIC searches should examine both forms.

notes.text: From Old Iranian *patigāma. On mng. 1a.1 cf. J. C. Greenfield 1982b. In what is probably a majority of instances this lexeme has the connotation of an official or divine pronouncement as opposed to the otherwise unmarked mlh n.f. Given the distribution of meanings, it is clear that the usage "thing, matter" in Jewish texts reflects the double meaning of BH דָּבָר.
